title: Lisnagaver & Rasharkin
standfirst: Nineteenth-century records document several Glasgow households around Lisnagaver, Gortahar and Kilrea. Their shared older parentage, and any route back to Larne or Inishrush, remain open.
question: Can the documented Lisnagaver, Gortahar and Kilrea households be joined by a record that names their older parents, rather than by shared surname, locality, or DNA alone?
answer: Alexander’s probable father is John Glasgow, farmer, named in John-867’s 1846 marriage: Nancy’s probate citation and independently documented Glasgow birth surnames favour a common paternal sibling group. No record names Alexander’s own father directly. The Thomas–Daniel family is independently proved but is not joined to Alexander by a parent statement. The Desertoghill and Larne identities remain separate hypotheses. Older Alexander’s new uncertain Larne father belongs to that competing family model; the record-defined John remains younger Alexander-951’s leading father comparison.

chapters.title: Larne and Inishrush: James’s possible sons Adam and Alexander
body: Glasgow-1509, the older Larne ropemaker, is selected as the uncertain working father of Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902). This adopts the named-family comparison already tested in September. Adam’s gravestone age implies birth about 1758; James’s reported 1737 birth would give an ordinary age-21 generation. The original 1773 affidavit independently places the Larne James’s birth before October 1743, although it does not prove the reported 1737 year. Adam’s proved son James (Glasgow-3903) supplies limited positive naming support. James is a documented adult with a trade and property trail, making him a more useful provisional father than the recordless [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) placeholder. No record names Adam as his child, and the naming argument is weak rather than corroboration of a parent clause.

The same James is selected, with very low confidence, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. On the reported 1737 and estimated 1770 years, James would be about 33 at Alexander’s birth. Making Adam, born about 1758, Alexander’s father instead produces a twelve-year interval. Alexander’s circa 1770 birth is only an estimate, so that calculation does not exclude an Adam father: Alexander could have been born later. However, fatherhood of Daniel by about 1795/96 places Alexander in a generation born by roughly 1775–1778, leaving two short successive generations in the Adam-to-Alexander model. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other.

A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved.

The two local 1740 Tamlaght Hugh households, including Glasgow-3931, and the older Adam-and-Maria naming model remain alternatives for Adam. A different unrecorded father remains possible. Neither Larne property succession nor the Inishrush household totals connect these generations. The 1831 return does not identify its unnamed occupants, and the later plot-29 succession is not evidence of James the ropemaker’s paternity. The shared [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) field is a recently created research placeholder, not evidence that Adam, older Alexander and Glasgow-1367 were brothers. It is not identified or merged with James. No father is extended to Glasgow-1367, and no unnamed extra generation is added.

Older Alexander is himself reconstructed chiefly from late descendant testimony naming Thomas’s parents as Alexander and Rosanna. The 2007 account and its copied 2020 restatement are one source tradition, not independent witnesses. Daniel and Thomas are proved brothers, but their father’s name is not established by a contemporary parent record. The new James father therefore depends on that reconstructed older Alexander account. Younger Glasgow-951 remains a separate, unresolved possible brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel; the record-defined Glasgow-4090 remains his leading current father comparison. This batch does not select older Alexander as younger Alexander’s father or place that younger family beneath James. No Rosanna surname or October 1822 death date is newly established. James’s own Glasgow-1505 and Glasgow-1499 ancestry alternatives and existing children retain their earlier assessments.

Two named father hypotheses are selected from existing research, with low/very low confidence. No new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. All existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics remain unchanged. Mothers are independently unassigned. The local model replaces the placeholder father only in these two selected views; captured WikiTree fields and rival parentage remain available. Counts describe retained profile accounts and conditional ancestry, not a proved pedigree.

evidence.label: Tamlaght gravestone: Adam died 30 June 1844 aged 86; Rose died 31 July 1833 aged 66; photograph and transcription
Registry of Deeds, ropewalk lease 10 September 1760, registered 24 November 1763: Belfast ropemaker taking Gardenmore, Larne
Registry of Deeds, assignment 28 March 1768: matching Larne ropewalk and lease term
Registry memorial 204122, 14 May 1766: James Glasgow, Larne ropemaker, witness
Registry affidavit sworn 27 October 1773, registered 15 November: Larne gentleman aged upwards of thirty
Genes Reunited thread 465937: 2007 descendant account, later copied; previously reviewed derivative testimony, not contemporary proof
1740 Protestant Householders’ Return, Macafee transcription: two Tamlaght Hugh households, no stated kinship

chapters.title: A local network before the later families
body: The study keeps nearby Inishrush and Bann Valley material as comparison evidence, not as an inherited pedigree. Adam and John at Inishrush may be related, but no inspected record calls them brothers or names a shared parent.
The 1831 household return records separate Adam and John Glasgow households in Inishrush; it does not list household members by name.

chapters.title: Alexander and Mary’s documented family
body: Baptisms, the complete 1851 household and later marriages document Alexander Glasgow and Mary McCaughan and six children. Their descendant evidence places a tested line in R-FT20271.

John Glasgow, farmer, is Alexander’s probable father through Nancy’s reconstructed sibling group. Her newly inspected 1891 death notice gives about 75, conflicting with the age in her will; it confirms her Plattsburgh death and funeral but names no parents. The Glenleslie Nancy who died in 1847 is a different woman. Mary McCaughan’s parents remain unresolved.

PRONI reported no Glasgow or surname-variant mention under AG 57714 on 15 October 2026. The original enquiry prioritised Second Portglenone marriages, 1834–1838, but the result does not enumerate its actual record coverage. The separate Ballymoney Reformed Presbyterian family-register search, 1804–1844, is AG 57828 and remains outstanding. Neither the negative search nor the outstanding request changes the parentage assessment; the Lisnagaver rent-roll and map copy requests are also unresolved.

evidence.label: PRONI outcome, scope and outstanding requests — 15 October 2026

chapters.title: John and Margaret at Lisnagaver
body: The 1846 marriage, 1851 household and family memorial establish John Glasgow, Margaret Garvin, their children and John’s brother Samuel.

John’s original 1846 marriage names his father John Glasgow, farmer. The record-defined father is represented by Glasgow-4090; identifying him with the 1796 Desertoghill occupier or Glenleslie John is a separate unproved step.

chapters.title: Thomas and Daniel are brothers
body: Daniel’s will calls Thomas his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew. Daniel Neely’s marriage names Thomas as father.
That evidence proves the brotherhood and nephew relationship, but does not name Thomas and Daniel’s parents or prove Alexander was their brother.

Two Belfast death notices identify [Daniel Glasgow](/people/glasgow-3896.html) at Church Street, Kilrea, on 16 October 1871. They give age 73; his civil registration gives 75. These repeated notices corroborate the death date and address but leave a two-year birth-age discrepancy. They do not identify the brothers’ parents or connect them to Alexander’s family.

chapters.title: Later documented continuations
body: Daniel Neely Glasgow and Mary Jane Boyd’s marriage and original birth returns document daughters Sarah Taylor and Elizabeth Boyd. Mary Ann Glasgow’s marriage names Alexander as her father and later records continue the Elder household.

The original 6 January 1892 Belfast notice names [Jane Graham](/people/graham-21720.html) as wife of [Robert Glasgow](/people/glasgow-938.html). She died on 28 December at 534 Gallowgate, Glasgow, aged 51. The notice adds “formerly of Rasharkin” after Robert’s name. The exact death date and address strongly match Jane’s existing profile and support the couple’s Scottish continuation; the phrase is not assigned exclusively to Jane. It supplies no parents and does not identify the Robert in the separate 1861 neighbour report.
These continuations do not settle the older Glasgow-parentage question.

evidence.label: Jane Graham, wife of Robert: Belfast News-Letter, 6 January 1892, p.1

chapters.title: Lisnagaver newspaper context
body: The Belfast News-Letter of 5 June 1829 lists No. 2324, Alex. Glasgow, Lisnagaver, among applications to register freeholds under 10 Geo IV c. 8; the description gives lands in Kilconway barony and Lisnagaver townland. This is an application only: no age, kinship, admission or successful registration is stated.

The original page is now inspected, resolving the earlier access gap. [Alexander Glasgow-951](/people/glasgow-951.html) and [older Alexander Glasgow-3904](/people/glasgow-3904.html) remain compatible applicant candidates. The conflicting age estimates remain open; no parentage confidence changes.

A 7 January 1861 report names Robt. Glasgow as a Lisnagaver neighbour who warned James M’Caughern before a house collapse and narrowly escaped. [Robert Glasgow-938](/people/glasgow-938.html) and [Robert Glasgow-3449](/people/glasgow-3449.html) remain compatible candidates. No age, kinship or property bridge is stated.

clusters.title: Alexander Glasgow and Mary McCaughan
clusters.summary: Baptisms, the complete 1851 household and later marriages document the couple and six children. A tested descendant is in R-FT20271.
clusters.boundary: Alexander’s parents, the named ancestor shared with James J, and his exact relationship to Thomas and Daniel remain unresolved. The 1888 death remains probable, with age and informant identity unresolved.

clusters.title: John Glasgow and Margaret Garvin
clusters.summary: The 1846 marriage, 1851 household and family memorial establish the couple, their children and John’s brother Samuel.
clusters.boundary: The older father John is named but not securely identified with an existing profile.

clusters.title: Thomas and Daniel Glasgow
clusters.summary: Daniel’s will calls Thomas his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew; the nephew’s marriage names Thomas as father.
clusters.boundary: The records do not name the brothers’ parents or prove Alexander was their brother.

clusters.title: Daniel Neely Glasgow and Mary Jane Boyd
clusters.summary: The marriage and original birth returns document the couple and daughters Sarah Taylor and Elizabeth Boyd Glasgow.
clusters.boundary: Their later migration evidence does not resolve the older Glasgow parentage question.

clusters.title: Mary Ann Glasgow and Robert Elder
clusters.summary: Mary’s marriage names Alexander Glasgow as her father and later Gortahar records continue the Elder household.
clusters.boundary: Only catalogue people with public dossiers are linked here; unresolved later children remain research subjects.

clusters.title: Inishrush collateral leads
clusters.summary: Family-register, census, tithe and marriage clues identify Adam and John as meaningful comparison leads beside, not within, the later Lisnagaver households.
clusters.boundary: No document proves a bridge to Lisnagaver or Bann Valley families; Adam and John may be brothers, cousins or unrelated namesakes.

proved: Daniel and Thomas are brothers; Daniel Neely is Thomas’s son and Daniel’s nephew.
Alexander and Mary’s household, John and Margaret’s household, and Mary Ann’s father statement are documented.
supported: Nancy’s citation and independent surname records favour Alexander and John sharing a Glasgow father; John farmer is the probable father, without a direct statement for Alexander.
hypothesis: Adam and John of Inishrush may be brothers or cousins.
The Gortereghy, Drumadarragh and Finvoy McCaughan networks are candidate routes to Mary’s parentage.
unresolved: Alexander’s mother and a proved parentage bridge to Thomas and Daniel are missing; the probable John father is not automatically the Desertoghill man.
No record proves a Lisnagaver descent from Inishrush, Larne or another Irish cluster.

gaps.why: An original parent statement in Nancy’s reconstructed sibling group could strengthen or redirect the father inference without relying entirely on her probate petition.

gaps.title: Resolve the Inishrush household relationships
gaps.why: Church, lease and succession records could distinguish Adam–John brotherhood from cousin or namesake alternatives.

gaps.title: Identify a documented male-line comparator
gaps.why: No Kilwaughter kit has an SNP result yet, so nothing places that documented family inside R-FT20271. A Big Y-700 upgrade of the reported Robert c.1710 line would show whether it is in that branch at all; a John-867 male line would test the brotherhood with Alexander directly, but none is known. No result can name an ancestor by itself.

sources_note: Original 1846 Irish marriage, Nancy’s will and probate citation, the newly inspected 1891 newspaper death notice, and Irish census and family records underpin the conclusions. The linked people pages distinguish records from identity hypotheses and record the bounded searches completed on 29 September 2026. The 1871 Belfast death notices repeat one account; their age of 73 is retained alongside the civil-register age of 75.
